analysis.one_liner: Strips the first-generic exclusivity reward from companies paid by brand drugmakers to delay generic competition.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan backing from 12 senators, the bill died in the Senate Health Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, the first generic company to challenge a brand-name drug's patents can win a 180-day head start as the only generic on the market. The FAIR Generics Act would take that reward away from any generic company that signs a settlement with the brand-name maker agreeing to keep its drug off the market, and would let other generic challengers claim the first-filer spot instead. It would also require the parties to file the details of any such deal with the Health and Human Services Department within ten business days, and would narrow the window for patent lawsuits over a generic approval.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, consumers, and anyone who pays for prescriptions — households, employers, Medicare, and Medicaid — would benefit if settlements that pay generic makers to stay off the market no longer work. Cheaper generic versions of a drug typically enter sooner and at much lower prices, and the bill would ensure that when the first generic challenger settles without a real patent fight, other generics can step in and launch.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers and payers buying brand-name drugs

how_it_helps.text: Disqualifies a generic applicant from the valuable 180-day exclusivity period if it signs a 'disqualifying agreement' with the brand-name drug company or patent holder to delay seeking approval or launching its generic.

Expands 'first applicant' status so that other generic challengers who were sued and either won, had the case dismissed, or were never sued at all can claim the exclusivity and launch — even if they filed later than a challenger who settled.

If a settlement names a marketing date, the generic cannot launch before the earlier of that agreed date or 180 days after another first-filer launches, closing a way for deal parties to control the timeline.
Requires the parties to a delay agreement to file its full terms with the Secretary of Health and Human Services within ten business days, so the deal cannot stay hidden from regulators.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug companies lose their most lucrative tool for extending monopoly pricing after patents expire: paying the generic challenger to stay off the market. Generic companies that have been collecting settlement payments lose that revenue stream, and patent holders face a tighter window to sue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drugmakers and settled generic firms

drawbacks.text: Expanding first-filer status beyond the first challenger could weaken the incentive that drives the earliest, most aggressive patent challenges, since a later filer could now win the 180-day prize without having taken the initial risk.

Settlements are not always anticompetitive — some let a generic launch before the patent expires in ways a court fight might not. The bill's bright-line disqualification would bar many of those deals too.
The deal notifications filed with HHS would be exempt from public disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act, visible to Congress and regulators but not to the public or press.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core fix targets a well-documented practice that keeps prescription prices high: brand-name makers compensating generic challengers to delay competition. The costs are real but modest — some genuinely pro-consumer settlements would be swept up in the ban, the first-filer incentive could be dulled, and the confidentiality of the filed deals limits public oversight. On balance the bill's main effect is lower prices for consumers, and its design trade-offs are the kind an honest supporter would acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or markup, so it died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Bingaman (D-NM) introduced the FAIR Generics Act on November 16, 2011, joined on the day of introduction by Sens. David Vitter (R-LA), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), and Sherrod Brown (D-OH).
Twelve senators cosponsored the bill: 10 Democrats, 1 Republican, and 1 Independent.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off because the bill died: they kept the ability to settle patent challenges by paying generic companies to stay off the market, preserving higher prices on their drugs. Generic firms that collect those settlement payments also kept the arrangement, while consumers continued paying brand-name prices for drugs whose patents were no longer being seriously contested.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and generic firms with delay deals

against.role: Major industry facing loss of pay-for-delay settlement revenue

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan in form — 12 cosponsors including one Republican and one Independent — but every recorded action after referral involved the Democratic-controlled Senate, whose committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill would take away their main tool for extending monopoly pricing past a patent's effective end: paying the generic challenger to stay off the market. Consumers pay the difference in the form of years of brand-name prices for drugs whose patents are no longer seriously contested.

Generic challengers who fight patents in court would gain — they could claim the 180-day exclusivity even if they were not the first to file. But generic firms that profit by taking settlement payments from brand-name companies would lose that revenue and be barred from first-filer status.

industries.industry: Health insurers, employers, and public programs like Medicare and Medicaid
industries.note: Earlier generic entry under a bill like this lowers drug costs for insurers, employer health plans, and government programs, savings that ultimately flow to premiums and taxpayers.
